text:
OET Speaking by Dr Amr Akmal




Introduction:
If you are seeing the patient for the first time:
  • Good morning. My name is Dr Amr and I will be looking after you today. How would you like me to
    address you? Nice to see you X. Please have a seat.
  • What would you prefer I call you?
  • Could I just confirm your name, please?
  • Good afternoon. Please be seated. My name is Amr. I’m one of the doctors working here in the
    clinic/ED, and I will be taking care of you/your daughter/son/kid today.
  •   How can I help you?
  •   Tell me what brings you in today.
  •   What’s brought you in today?
  •   Can you tell me what seems to be the problem?
  •   What’s been happening?

If you have already seen the patient before:
  •   How are you doing? It’s nice to see you again.
  •   Hello, it’s nice to see you again. How have you been doing since we last met?
  •   Hello, it’s nice to see you again. How has your child been doing since the last visit?
  •   I understand that you are coming/here today for/to review the results of your blood test/pathology.
  •   I understand you’re here today to review your test results.
  •   I see you’ve come back to discuss the results of your blood tests.
  •   We’re meeting today to follow up on your symptoms.

If examination is already done:
  •   Thank you for waiting.
  •   Thank you for letting me examine you.
  •   Thank you for your cooperation.
  •   Thank you for your patience.
  •   Thanks for bearing with me.
  •   I appreciate your cooperation during the examination.
  •   Now that I’ve had a chance to examine you…
  •   Having examined you, I’d like to explain what I’ve found.
  •   Based on my examination, I can reassure you that…
  •   On examination, I noticed…
  •   The examination suggests that…
  • Thank you for waiting. Now that I’ve had a chance to examine you, I can reassure you that the
    findings are generally normal. Let me explain what this means.
  • I’ve completed your examination, and I’d like to talk you through what I found and discuss the next
    steps.



                                                                                                            1
 
OET Speaking by Dr Amr Akmal



  • I know you’ve been anxious. Having examined you, I didn’t find anything alarming, which is
    reassuring.


Talking about the patient’s condition:
Asking more about the symptoms:
  • I think you’ve been referred to me by your GP because you’ve been experiencing some symptoms
    with your abdomen. I’ve got your notes here, but perhaps you can tell me in your own words what
    seems to be the problem. What’s brought you here today?
  • I have your notes here, but it would be good to hear things from your perspective. How all this
    started, what treatments you've had, anything you think I should be aware of.
  • I’ve got your notes here, but perhaps you can tell me in your own words how all this started, any
    treatment you've had so far and anything else you feel I should be aware of.
  • I understand from your notes here that you have been recently experiencing/suffering from X. I
    would prefer to hear from you in your own words about your condition/I want you to tell me a little
    bit more about your condition. How did it start and how does it feel?/Can you give me some
    background about your condition?/Tell me more about the symptoms you’ve been experiencing.
  •   Before we go further, I’d like to ask you a few questions.
  •   To understand this better, can I ask you some questions?
  •   I understand you’re in pain. I’ll ask you a few questions first if that is okay.
  •   I will talk to you about that in a minute, but first, I would like to ask you about.
  •   I'll speak to you a bit more about those symptoms in a moment, but what I'd like to know first is.
  •   You’ve mentioned that you have been suffering from pain, is that right? Could you tell me more
      about the pain?
  •   For how long have you been experiencing that pain?
  •   Do you know what might be causing the pain?/What do you think might be causing that pain?
  •   Do you feel/believe there is anything that can aggravate or alleviate this condition/the pain?
  •   How can you describe it?/How does it feel?/What does it feel like?
  •   How often do you feel that pain?
  •   Where exactly does it hurt?
  •   Is that pain constant or comes and goes/or happens on and off?
  •   Does it radiate to any other place?
  •   On a scale of zero to ten, where zero is no pain at all and ten is the worst possible pain, how would
      you rate your pain?/where would you say the pain is?/can you tell me how severe your pain is?
  • If zero is no pain and ten is the worst pain, where would you place your pain?/How severe is your
    pain on a scale of zero to ten?
  • Are you/Has your child been experiencing any other symptoms? Any headaches? Have you noticed
    anything abnormal on him/her?
  • Sorry, I missed what you said about your pain. Can you please repeat that?
  • But then you started to develop other symptoms?



                                                                                                              2
 
OET Speaking by Dr Amr Akmal



Asking about history:
  • Have you ever felt anything like that before?
  • Have you ever experienced anything like that before?
  • Have you been taking any medications for this condition? Did it get any better?/So, as far as I
    understand, you are not taking/not compliant to your medications anymore. Is that right?
  • What did your doctor tell you about the diagnosis then?
  • What treatment did you have then?
  • Does any of your family members suffer from any similar condition or any other medical
    problems?/Do you have any family history of any medical condition?
  • Can I ask you some more/a few questions regarding your past medical history if you don’t mind?

Asking for patient’s permission to perform examination:
  •   Would it be okay if I examine you now?
  •   Would you mind if I examine you now?
  •   May I examine you now?
  •   I’d like to examine you, if that’s okay.
  •   If you’re comfortable, I’ll examine you.
  •   To help me understand what’s going on, would it be okay if I examine you?
  •   This will only take a few minutes, and I’ll explain each step as we go.

Requesting investigations:
  •   To get to the bottom of the problem, we need to run some tests.
  •   To get to the bottom of what’s going on, I’d recommend doing some tests.
  •   Given your symptoms, imaging may help us rule out inner ear or nerve-related causes.
  •   This is a precautionary step to make sure we don’t miss anything.
  • At this stage, it’s too early to be certain about a final diagnosis. We’ll need to run some tests,
    including blood tests and liver function tests, to rule out other conditions that can present in a
    similar way.
  • At the moment, it’s too early to confirm a final diagnosis. We need to do some tests, such as blood
    tests and liver function tests, to exclude other conditions that may cause similar symptoms.
  •   An X-ray would help us check the bones and surrounding structures.
  •   I’d recommend an X-ray to rule out any structural problems.
  •   An X-ray is a simple test that can help us identify any abnormalities.
  •   I’d suggest an ultrasound to assess the area more closely.
  •   A CT scan can give us detailed images to help rule out more serious causes.
  •   To get a clearer picture of what’s going on, I’d recommend an MRI. This is mainly to rule out other
      causes and for reassurance. How does that sound to you?

Reaching a diagnosis:
  • Well, thank you for all that background. That's really given me a good idea of what we need to do.
  • Thank you for sharing this information with me. It really helps me understand your situation.


                                                                                                            3
 
OET Speaking by Dr Amr Akmal



  • From what you’ve told me and from the examination, this looks like aphthous ulcers.
  • Based on your history and initial examination, it appears that you have something/what’s called X
  • What do you already know about your condition?/Have you ever heard of it before?/Have the
    doctors told you anything about your condition and the treatment options? Are you familiar with
    this condition?
  • Would it be okay if I briefly explain what this condition means?
  • Let me explain this in simple terms.
  • We’ll come back to that in a moment, but first, would it be okay if I briefly explain what this condition
    means?
  •   I’ll address that shortly, but first, may I explain what this condition means?
  •   Before we go into that, would it be alright if I explain the condition in simple terms?
  •   I’ll explain that in a moment. First, let me briefly explain what this condition means.
  •   In simple words, bronchial asthma is a lung condition, where.
  •   In simple terms, bronchial asthma is a long-term lung condition where the airways become inflamed
      and narrow, making it difficult to breathe.
  • I’ll try to explain this in simple terms
  • Do you want me to go over that again?
  • Let me see if I can summarize what you’ve said


Giving advice and discussing treatment:
Discussing treatment and assuring patients:
  • Now that we’ve discussed the symptoms and signs of your condition, I would next like to talk to you
    now about the management plan.
  • Now that we’ve talked about your symptoms and examination findings, I’d like to discuss the
    management plan with you. Let’s move on to how we can manage this condition.
  • There are several treatment options available, and I’ll explain each one to you.
  • We have a few ways to manage this, and we’ll choose what suits you best.
  • The good news is that this condition is usually self-limiting.
  • The good news is that this condition is completely manageable with the right treatment.
  • It is contagious, but we can take steps to prevent it from spreading.
  • Most people start to feel better within about two weeks and can gradually return to their normal
    activities.
  •   You should be able to get back to work in around two weeks, depending on your recovery.
  •   Once you start the treatment, you should notice a gradual improvement.
  •   As long as you take the medications as prescribed and get enough rest, you should recover well.
  •   Rest will play a big role in your recovery.

Sympathizing with the patient:
  • I’m really sorry you’re going through this.


                                                                                                                4
 
OET Speaking by Dr Amr Akmal



  •   That sounds really upsetting for you.
  •   I can see how worried you are.
  •   Anyone in your situation would feel the same.
  •   It’s completely normal to feel this way.
  •   It’s completely understandable to feel this way.
  •   I understand why this is concerning for you.
  •   I’m sorry to hear that.
  •   I understand your concerns/worries.
  •   I understand this must be a hard time for you.
  •   That must have been very difficult/so hard/tough/distressing for you.
  •   I can imagine how stressful this has been.
  •   It sounds like this has been a tough time for your family.
  •   You’ve been dealing with a lot.
  •   As a parent, it’s completely understandable to feel anxious.

Drawing the patient’s attention in a positive way:
  • I know this is hard to hear about your son/daughter, but with the medication and proper rest at
    home, she/he should start to improve.
  • I see that this can be a bit scary, but this is the best treatment option for your case.
  • Right now, the most important thing is helping you recover.
  • Let’s concentrate on what we can do to help you feel better.
  •   I want to reassure you that this condition is quite common.
  •   The good news is that this condition is very manageable.
  •   We see this quite often, and most patients do very well.
  •   Based on my experience, patients usually recover well.
  •   This condition is quite common, and most patients recover fully with proper treatment.
  •   You seem a little uncomfortable about commencing on the medical treatment. Is that right?
  •   You seem a little hesitant about starting the medication. Is that right? Can you tell me what is
      worrying you the most?
  • Is there anything in particular that’s worrying you about the medication?
  • We’ll be monitoring you closely throughout the treatment.
  • We’ll monitor you closely while you’re on this medication, and we will deal promptly with any side
    effects if thy happen.
  • We’ll take this step by step together.

Checking clarity and understanding:
  •   Does that make sense?
  •   Is that clear so far?
  •   Am I explaining this clearly?
  •   Do you understand what I mean?
  •   Does this sound clear to you?



                                                                                                         5
 
OET Speaking by Dr Amr Akmal



  •   Can I just check that I’ve explained everything clearly?
  •   Could you tell me, in your own words, what you’ve understood so far?
  •   Would you like me to go over that again?
  •   Shall I explain that in a different way?
  •   Are you comfortable with the treatment plan we’ve discussed?
  •   Do you feel clear about how to take the medication?
  •   Is everything clear about when and how to use the treatment?
  •   Do you have any questions about the treatment?
  •   Please feel free to stop me if anything isn’t clear.
  •   If anything doesn’t make sense, just let me know.
  •   What questions do you have at this stage?
  •   How do you feel about what we’ve discussed?
  •   Is there anything you’re still unsure or worried about?
  •   Does this address your main concerns?
  •   Does this answer your question?

Dealing with serious conditions:
  •   I’ve received your pathology report.
  •   I’m afraid the results are more serious than we were hoping for.
  •   The pathology results show that the lesion is malignant, which means it is cancer.
  •   The tests confirm a diagnosis of colon cancer.
  •   Unfortunately, your condition appears to a little bit more serious than we think.
  •   The results show no evidence of colon cancer.
  •   I can imagine this news is very upsetting.
  •   I can imagine how upsetting this must be for you.
  •   I can understand how frustrating this situation is.
  •   I can see how distressed you are.
  •   That must be very difficult for you.
  •   I understand this is a lot to take in. Please take your time and tell me what’s going through your mind
      right now?
  •   Please take your time. What’s going through your mind right now?
  •   There is a lot we can do to manage this.
  •   You are not alone, and we will support you through this.
  •   Effective treatments are available.
  •   Given the nature of the condition, I’d recommend referring you to an oncologist as soon as possible.
  •   Early specialist involvement is important.
  • The good news is that it was detected at an early stage. This significantly improves the chances of
    successful treatment. Treatment is expected to be effective.
  • I understand the idea of surgery can be frightening.
  • Based on current evidence, surgery offers the best chance of cure.
  • Your surgeon will discuss the risks and benefits in detail.



                                                                                                                6
 
OET Speaking by Dr Amr Akmal



  •   What are your main concerns right now?
  •   Do you have any questions about the diagnosis or next steps?
  •   Would you like me to explain anything again?
  •   I’m afraid the results are more serious than we were hoping for. The biopsy confirms colon cancer. I
      understand this is difficult news, and it’s completely normal to feel overwhelmed. The good news is
      that it was detected early, and there are effective treatment options available. I’d recommend
      referring you to an oncologist to discuss the next steps. What concerns you most at the moment?

Dealing with anxious/stubborn patients:
  • I understand that you might not want to stop taking your sleeping pills, but believe me, I’m
    concerned about your health and general wellbeing.
  • I understand why you feel reluctant to stop your sleeping tablets. My concern is about your long-
    term health, as these medications can be addictive and can also cause many undesirable side effects.
  • Would it be okay if I explain why I’m recommending a change?
  • I understand that you might not feel comfortable about taking this medication. Is that right? Can
    you give me a reason for that? What is making you so concerned or worried? What is
    worrying/concerning you the most?
  • Based on clinical guidelines and experience with similar patients, this treatment is considered one
    of the most effective options. Ultimately, the decision is yours, but I’d strongly recommend this
    approach.
  •   Taking your medication regularly gives us the best chance of controlling your symptoms.
  •   As we know, when it comes to treatment, early intervention is key.
  •   Early treatment usually leads to better outcomes.
  •   I completely understand your worries and concerns, but if we work together and follow the plan,
      we have a very good chance of controlling this condition. My aim is to support you and help you feel
      better.
  • This forms an important part of the treatment plan and is expected to help.
  • If this were a member of my own family, I would feel comfortable recommending this treatment.
  • I understand this is very frustrating, especially when your child is in pain. I can see you’re trying to
    help, and I respect that. My priority is his safety, and that’s why I don’t recommend this option.
  • Well, the benefits generally outweigh any risks, as long as you don't exceed the recommended dose.
    We’ll monitor you closely and adjust the dose if needed.
  • I wouldn't advise/recommend that actually and I’m happy to explain why.

Dealing with patient asking for unnecessary action:
 Sick leave/Medical certificate
  • I understand you’re hoping for some time off.
  • My hands are tied by medical guidelines.
  • I have to work within medical regulations.
  • I can only issue a certificate when it’s clinically indicated.


                                                                                                               7
 
OET Speaking by Dr Amr Akmal



 •   At the moment, there’s no medical basis for sick leave.
 •   From a medical point of view, you’re fit to work.
 •   I wouldn’t be doing you any favours by issuing a certificate unnecessarily.
 •   I wouldn’t feel comfortable certifying this medically.
 • What I can do is help you manage your symptoms.
 • We can look at other ways to support you.
 • I can understand why you’re asking for a medical certificate. Unfortunately, at this stage there isn’t
   a medical indication for sick leave. My hands are tied by clinical guidelines, but I’m happy to discuss
   ways to help you manage your symptoms.
 • I appreciate this is frustrating, but I wouldn’t feel comfortable issuing a certificate without a clear
   medical reason. I want to be honest and fair with you.
 • At the moment, you’re medically fit to work. However, if your condition worsens, please come back
   and we can reassess.
 • At the moment, there’s no medical indication for sick leave. However, I can help you manage your
   symptoms and feel better. There are several proven strategies to cope with stress, and many patients
   with a similar condition have found significant improvement using them. Would you like me to talk
   you through some of these strategies?
 • I understand why you’re asking for sick leave, but medically there’s no indication for it right now.
   What I can do is help you manage your symptoms. There are effective, evidence-based ways to cope
   with stress, and many patients in a similar situation have improved with these approaches. Would
   you like me to talk you through some of these strategies?

Hospital admission
 • It’s completely understandable to want to be on the safe side.
 • At this stage, hospital admission wouldn’t add any benefit.
 • Right now, admission isn’t medically justified.
 • From a clinical point of view, it’s safe to manage this at home.
 • Keeping you in hospital wouldn’t change the management.
 • My decision is guided by clinical guidelines.
 • Admitting you unnecessarily could actually do more harm than good.
 • What we can do instead is…
 • We’ll arrange close follow-up to check on your progress and how you’re responding to treatment.
 • If anything changes, you should come back immediately.
 • I can understand why you’d feel safer staying in hospital. The good news is that you’re stable and
   there are no red flags, so admission wouldn’t add any benefit. We can safely manage this at home,
   and I’ll explain exactly what to watch out for.”
 • I can see you want to be on the safe side for your child. At the moment, he doesn’t meet the criteria
   for hospital admission, and keeping him here unnecessarily could expose him to other risks. I’ll make
   sure you know when to come back if things change.”




                                                                                                             8
 
OET Speaking by Dr Amr Akmal



  • I appreciate your concern, but I have to go by medical guidelines. Right now, admission isn’t
    medically justified. What I can do is arrange follow-up and give you clear instructions on when to
    seek urgent help.

Referring the patient:
  • Also, I would recommend referring you to/arranging an appointment with a dietician for a specialist
    opinion. They have specific expertise in managing this condition. A dietitian can help tailor a plan
    that suits your lifestyle and medical needs.
  • How would you feel about seeing a dietitian? Seeking specialist input can be very helpful in
    managing this condition.
  • You’ll receive appropriate care from someone with expertise in this condition.
  • Getting expert advice at this stage can make a big difference.

Taking about lifestyle improvement:
 General questions:
  • How do you feel about making some lifestyle changes, such as exercising more or reducing alcohol?
  • Have you ever thought about adopting a healthier lifestyle?
  • Have you considered starting a regular exercise program or following a healthier diet?
  • I think introducing some healthy habits now could be very beneficial.

 Body weight:
  • Would it be okay if we talked about your weight for a moment?
  • I’d like to discuss your weight and what steps you might take to manage it.
  • I want to check how comfortable you feel about making some changes to your weight.
  • Excess weight can sometimes worsen conditions like blood pressure and diabetes.
  • Losing even a small amount of weight can make a big difference to your health.
  • We can work together on a plan that suits your lifestyle.
  • Would you be open to seeing a dietitian?
  • We could start with simple changes like portion control or light exercise.

 Smoking:
  • Would it be okay if we talked a little about your smoking?
  • Do you mind if I ask you a few questions about your smoking habits?
  • How many cigarettes do you smoke on an average day?
  • On average, how many cigarettes do you smoke a day?
  • Do you mind if I ask how many cigarettes you smoke per day?
  •   Have you ever thought about cutting down or quitting?
  •   From what you’ve told me, smoking may be contributing to your cough/high blood pressure.
  •   Smoking can irritate the airways and slow down recovery, which might explain your symptoms.
  •   Quitting can significantly reduce your risk of heart and lung disease.
  •   If you decide to quit, we can support you through the process. There are several effective options,
      including nicotine patches, gum, medications, and counselling.



                                                                                                            9
 
OET Speaking by Dr Amr Akmal



 • We can take this step by step. You don’t have to do it alone.
 • Even cutting down is a good first step. We can review your progress at your next visit.
 • What do you think would be the hardest part about quitting?/What’s stopping you from trying at
   the moment? Many people worry about withdrawal or weight gain. We can manage that together.

Alcohol intake:
 • Would it be okay if we talked briefly about your alcohol intake?
 • Can I ask a few questions about your drinking habits?
 • I’d like to ask you a few questions about your alcohol consumption, if that’s alright.
 • Do you mind if I ask about how much alcohol you usually drink?
 • On average, how much do you drink in a week?
 •   Alcohol can sometimes affect conditions like blood pressure, diabetes, and liver health.
 •   In your case, cutting down could really help improve your symptoms.
 •   Have you ever thought about cutting down?
 •   I understand this might be difficult, but even reducing gradually can make a significant difference to
     your health.
 • If you’d like, I can refer you to a specialist or support service.

Checking for understanding and insights:
 • What do you think about that?
 • How do you feel about that?
 • Do you think you could try this?
 • How comfortable do you feel with this approach?
 • Do you feel this is something you could manage?


Recapping and closure:
 •   Do you have any further questions or concerns regarding what we’ve discussed?
 •   Is there anything else that I can help you with?
 •   Would you like me to clarify anything we’ve talked about?
 •   To summarise, we’ve talked about X, and it’s important to remember X.
 •   Just to recap: we discussed X, and the key points are X.
 •   In summary, the main things we’ve covered are X, and what’s most important is X.
 •   I hope that I’ve made things clearer to you and I’ll give you some brochures to take home, which
     explain your condition and treatment options.
 • Just to make sure I’ve explained everything clearly, could you tell me in your own words what the
   next steps are?
 •   Can you tell me in your own words what you understand about the next steps?
 •   Please don’t hesitate to reach out if anything changes.
 •   If anything changes or you have concerns, please get in touch.
 •   I wish you a speedy recovery.
 •   I hope you get better so soon.


                                                                                                              10
 
OET Speaking by Dr Amr Akmal



 • I’ll give you a leaflet with further information about your condition, possible symptoms, and the next
   steps. Does that sound okay?


Setting a follow-up visit:
 • I would like to review/see you again in 2 weeks to check up on your progress and see how you are
   responding to the treatment.
 • I’d like to see you again in two weeks to review your progress and check how you’re responding to
   the treatment.
 •   We should schedule a follow-up in two weeks to monitor your response to the treatment
 •   I suggest you come back in a couple of weeks for a review.
 •   It would be good to see you again in two weeks to check how things are going.
 •   Let’s arrange a follow-up appointment in two weeks to assess your progress.


Common Role play scenarios:
Scenario 1: Patient/Relative Requesting Medication Without
Examination
     • Doctor: Good morning. Please have a seat. My name is Dr Amr, and I’ll be looking after
       you today. How can I help?
     • Patient/Relative: I’m here to get a prescription for my father. He’s not feeling well.
     • Doctor: I understand. Can you tell me a bit more about his symptoms and how long he’s
       been unwell?
     • Patient/Relative: He’s had a cough and fever for three days.
     • Doctor: I appreciate you coming in to help. However, I can only prescribe medication after
       examining him myself. This ensures we give the safest and most effective treatment.
     • Patient/Relative: So, you can’t give the medication?
     • Doctor: That’s right. Prescribing without seeing him could be risky, as I wouldn’t know his
       full medical status or potential reactions.
     • Patient/Relative: What can we do then?
     • Doctor: He can come in for an appointment today. If urgent, we’ll see him immediately.
       We could also arrange a telehealth consult, but a physical exam may still be needed
       depending on his symptoms.
     • Patient/Relative: Okay, that sounds good.
     • Doctor: Great. This is for his safety. Do you have any questions about this?

Scenario 2: Explaining a Diagnosis and Treatment Plan (e.g.,
Type 2 Diabetes)
     • Doctor: Hello Mr Smith. Please have a seat. I’d like to discuss the results of your recent
       tests.
     • Patient: Okay, doctor.


                                                                                                            11
 
OET Speaking by Dr Amr Akmal



    • Doctor: Your tests show that you have Type 2 Diabetes.
    • Patient: Oh… I see. What does that mean?
    • Doctor: It means your body isn’t producing enough insulin, or isn’t using it effectively, so
      your blood sugar levels are high.
    • Patient: Is it dangerous?
    • Doctor: If left unmanaged, it could affect your heart, kidneys, and eyes over time. The
      good news is it’s a manageable condition.
    • Patient: What do I need to do?
    • Doctor: Our main goal is to control your blood sugar. This usually involves medication,
      dietary changes, and regular exercise. We can also refer you to a dietician for a
      personalized plan.
    • Patient: Will I need insulin?
    • Doctor: Possibly, depending on how you respond to lifestyle changes and tablets. We’ll
      monitor your progress and adjust the treatment if needed.
    • Patient: I understand.
    • Doctor: Good. Do you have any questions or concerns about starting treatment?

Scenario 3: Discussing Sensitive Lifestyle Issues (e.g., Smoking,
Weight, Alcohol)
    • Doctor: Hello Ms Green. Please have a seat. I want to discuss your chronic cough. From
      your history, it seems smoking may be contributing to it.
    • Patient: Yes, I smoke about a pack a day.
    • Doctor: How do you feel about your smoking at the moment? Have you considered
      cutting down or quitting?
    • Patient: I’ve tried before, but it’s hard.
    • Doctor: I understand. Smoking irritates your airways, which makes coughing worse and
      increases infection risk. Quitting could help you breathe easier and feel more energetic.
    • Patient: I’m worried I can’t manage it.
    • Doctor: That’s normal. There are ways we can support you—nicotine replacement
      therapy, medications, and support groups. Would you like to explore some options?
    • Patient: Yes, I think that would help.
    • Doctor: Great. We’ll take it step by step, and you’ll have guidance along the way.

Scenario 4: Breaking Bad News
    • Doctor: Thank you for coming in today, Mr Taylor. I’m afraid I have some difficult news
      regarding your recent test results.
    • Patient: Oh… okay.
    • Doctor: Before I explain, what do you understand about your condition so far?
    • Patient: I know something is wrong with my lungs.
    • Doctor: The tests unfortunately show that you have advanced lung cancer.
    • Patient: Oh no…



                                                                                                     12
 
OET Speaking by Dr Amr Akmal



   • Doctor: I can see this is very upsetting. It’s completely understandable to feel
     overwhelmed.
   • Patient: What can be done now?
   • Doctor: We’ll discuss treatment options, which may include surgery, chemotherapy, and
     supportive care. We’ll also connect you with a palliative care team and support groups.
   • Patient: I don’t know if I can handle this.
   • Doctor: I understand. We’ll support you every step of the way. Do you have questions
     now, or would you like some time to process this?
   • Patient: I… need a moment.
   • Doctor: That’s okay. We can schedule another meeting with your family if you’d like, to
     discuss further.

Scenario 5: Managing an Angry/Demanding Patient or Relative
   • Doctor: Good afternoon, Mrs Lewis. I can see you’re upset. Please have a seat. Can you
     tell me what’s happened?
   • Patient/Relative: I’ve been waiting for over an hour! My son needs treatment now.
   • Doctor: I hear how frustrated you are about the waiting time. I understand this is very
     irritating, and I apologize for the delay.
   • Patient/Relative: This is unacceptable!
   • Doctor: We’ve had an unexpected emergency, which caused a backlog today. I assure you
     we are doing our best to see everyone safely.
   • Patient/Relative: He needs attention now.
   • Doctor: Let’s focus on your son. Can you tell me about his symptoms so we can prioritize
     his care?
   • Patient/Relative: He has a high fever and vomiting.
   • Doctor: Thank you for letting me know. We’ll see him immediately. I do need you to speak
     respectfully so we can provide the best care.
   • Patient/Relative: Alright…
   • Doctor: Thank you. We’ll take care of him now.


General Tips for All OET Speaking Role-Plays:
   • Establish Rapport: Start with a friendly greeting, introduce yourself, and confirm the
     patient's name.
   • Active Listening: Show you're listening by nodding, making eye contact, and using verbal
     affirmations ("I see," "Mm-hmm").
   • Empathy: Acknowledge the patient's feelings and concerns. Use phrases like "I
     understand this must be difficult for you," or "I can see why you're concerned."
   • Clear and Concise Language: Avoid medical jargon. Explain things in simple terms.
   • Structure Your Conversation:
      • Introduction: Greet, introduce, establish purpose.
      • Information Gathering: Ask open-ended questions.


                                                                                                13
 
OET Speaking by Dr Amr Akmal



        • Explanation/Education: Provide necessary information.
        • Reassurance/Support: Address concerns.
        • Action Plan: Discuss next steps.
        • Checking Understanding: "Does that make sense?" "Do you have any questions?"
        • Closing: Summarize, offer further assistance, say goodbye.

   • Time Management: Keep an eye on the clock (you'll have 5 minutes for the role-play).
     Practice staying within the time limit.
   • Professionalism: Maintain a professional and respectful tone throughout.
   • Confidence: Speak clearly and with conviction.


A Mental Checklist:
  1. Start Properly:
        ❖ The rule:
            •   Greet the patient
            •   Introduce yourself and your role
            •   Confirm the patient’s name
            •   State the purpose

        ❖ Example idioms:
            •   Good morning, I’m Dr Amr, one of the doctors working here today.
            •   Please have a seat.
            •   Could I just confirm your name, please?/How would you like me to address you?
            •   I understand you’re here today because …


  2. Open the Conversation:
        ❖ The rule: Use an open-ended opening question
        ❖ Example idioms:
            • How can I help you today?
            • What brings you in today?
            • I have got some notes here, but perhaps you can tell me in your own words what seems
                to be the problem.


  3. Explore Symptoms / Main Concern:
        ❖ The rule:
            • Ask about onset, duration, severity, associated symptoms
            • Use open questions first

        ❖ Example idioms:
            •   Before we go further, I’d like to ask you a few questions.
            •   To understand this better, can I ask you some questions?
            •   Could you tell me more about that?
            •   When did this start?


                                                                                                     14
 
OET Speaking by Dr Amr Akmal



            • How does it feel?


  4. Active Listening (Throughout):
        ❖ The rule: Use short verbal acknowledgements
        ❖ Example idioms:
            • I see.
            • Mm-hmm.
            • Right.


  5. Show Empathy After Every Complaint:
        ❖ Rule: No complaint without empathy
        ❖ Example idioms:
            • I’m sorry you’re going through this.
            • I can understand why this is concerning for you.
            • That must be quite uncomfortable


  6. Exclude Red Flags / Underlying Conditions:
        ❖ The rule: Ask focused questions to rule out serious causes
        ❖ Example idioms:
            • Have you ever been diagnosed with…?
            • Have you ever experienced any other symptoms such as…?


  7. Reach the Diagnosis (or Suspected Diagnosis):
        ❖ The rule:
            • State the diagnosis clearly and calmly
            • Use simple language

        ❖ Example idioms:
            • Based on what you’ve told me and my examination…
            • This seems to be most consistent with…


  8. Ask What the Patient Already Knows:
        ❖ The rule: Check prior knowledge before explaining the diagnosis
        ❖ Example idioms:
            • Have you heard of this condition before?
            • What do you already know about it?
            • Can you tell me in your own words what you already know about this condition?


  9. Explain the Condition:
        ❖ The rule: Give short, clear explanations. Avoid medical jargon
        ❖ Example idioms:
            • In simple terms, this means…
            • Basically, what happens is…


                                                                                              15
 
OET Speaking by Dr Amr Akmal




 10. Check Understanding After Explanation:
        ❖ Rule: Always check understanding after providing information or an explanation.
        ❖ Example idioms:
            • Does that make sense?
            • Is that clear so far?


 11. Discuss Investigations:
        ❖ The rule: Explain what the test is and why it’s needed
        ❖ Example idioms:
            • I’d recommend a simple test to rule out…
            • This will help us confirm…
            • To further investigate your symptoms, I’d recommend doing some blood tests.


 12. Check Understanding / Agreement for Tests:
        ❖ The rule: Obtain patient agreement
        ❖ Example idioms:
            • Is that okay with you?
            • Are you comfortable to proceed with this?


 13. Management / Treatment Plan:
        ❖ The rule: Explain what to do, how often, and for how long
        ❖ Example idioms:
            • What I’d suggest is…
            • The plan is to start with…


 14. Check Patient’s Opinion After Treatment:
        ❖ Rule: Always check for patient’s opinion after suggesting a treatment plan.
        ❖ Example idioms:
            • How do you feel about this plan?
            • Does that sound reasonable to you?


 15. Reassure and Give Prognosis:
        ❖ The rule: Normalize and reassure when appropriate
        ❖ Example idioms:
            • The good news is…
            • This usually improves on its own.


 16. Lifestyle Advice (If Relevant):
        ❖ The rule: Give practical, simple advice
        ❖ Example idioms:


                                                                                            16
 
OET Speaking by Dr Amr Akmal



            • Have you ever considered a healthier lifestyle?
            • It would help if you could…
            • Making a few lifestyle changes can reduce this.


 17. Ask for Questions:
        ❖ OET Rule: If the task does NOT start with a verb, ask the patient for further questions. The
           interlocutor’s question will usually guide you to address the remaining task points.

        ❖ Example idioms:
            • If the task says “the ulcer will resolve by itself in a few days”, ask the patient if they have
                any question. The interlocuter may then ask, “Will it go away on its own?”. Then you
                answer and safely cover that task.
            • Do you have any questions or concerns?
            • Is there anything else you’d like to ask?


 18. Close the Consultation:
        ❖ The rule:
            • Summarize
            • Offer follow-up
            • End politely

        ❖ Example idioms:
            • So, to summarise what we discussed today…
            • Please feel free to come back if things don’t improve.
            • Take care, and thank you for coming in.




                                                                                                                17

pages.text:
OET Speaking by Dr Amr Akmal




Introduction:
If you are seeing the patient for the first time:
  • Good morning. My name is Dr Amr and I will be looking after you today. How would you like me to
    address you? Nice to see you X. Please have a seat.
  • What would you prefer I call you?
  • Could I just confirm your name, please?
  • Good afternoon. Please be seated. My name is Amr. I’m one of the doctors working here in the
    clinic/ED, and I will be taking care of you/your daughter/son/kid today.
  •   How can I help you?
  •   Tell me what brings you in today.
  •   What’s brought you in today?
  •   Can you tell me what seems to be the problem?
  •   What’s been happening?

If you have already seen the patient before:
  •   How are you doing? It’s nice to see you again.
  •   Hello, it’s nice to see you again. How have you been doing since we last met?
  •   Hello, it’s nice to see you again. How has your child been doing since the last visit?
  •   I understand that you are coming/here today for/to review the results of your blood test/pathology.
  •   I understand you’re here today to review your test results.
  •   I see you’ve come back to discuss the results of your blood tests.
  •   We’re meeting today to follow up on your symptoms.

If examination is already done:
  •   Thank you for waiting.
  •   Thank you for letting me examine you.
  •   Thank you for your cooperation.
  •   Thank you for your patience.
  •   Thanks for bearing with me.
  •   I appreciate your cooperation during the examination.
  •   Now that I’ve had a chance to examine you…
  •   Having examined you, I’d like to explain what I’ve found.
  •   Based on my examination, I can reassure you that…
  •   On examination, I noticed…
  •   The examination suggests that…
  • Thank you for waiting. Now that I’ve had a chance to examine you, I can reassure you that the
    findings are generally normal. Let me explain what this means.
  • I’ve completed your examination, and I’d like to talk you through what I found and discuss the next
    steps.



                                                                                                            1

OET Speaking by Dr Amr Akmal



  • I know you’ve been anxious. Having examined you, I didn’t find anything alarming, which is
    reassuring.


Talking about the patient’s condition:
Asking more about the symptoms:
  • I think you’ve been referred to me by your GP because you’ve been experiencing some symptoms
    with your abdomen. I’ve got your notes here, but perhaps you can tell me in your own words what
    seems to be the problem. What’s brought you here today?
  • I have your notes here, but it would be good to hear things from your perspective. How all this
    started, what treatments you've had, anything you think I should be aware of.
  • I’ve got your notes here, but perhaps you can tell me in your own words how all this started, any
    treatment you've had so far and anything else you feel I should be aware of.
  • I understand from your notes here that you have been recently experiencing/suffering from X. I
    would prefer to hear from you in your own words about your condition/I want you to tell me a little
    bit more about your condition. How did it start and how does it feel?/Can you give me some
    background about your condition?/Tell me more about the symptoms you’ve been experiencing.
  •   Before we go further, I’d like to ask you a few questions.
  •   To understand this better, can I ask you some questions?
  •   I understand you’re in pain. I’ll ask you a few questions first if that is okay.
  •   I will talk to you about that in a minute, but first, I would like to ask you about.
  •   I'll speak to you a bit more about those symptoms in a moment, but what I'd like to know first is.
  •   You’ve mentioned that you have been suffering from pain, is that right? Could you tell me more
      about the pain?
  •   For how long have you been experiencing that pain?
  •   Do you know what might be causing the pain?/What do you think might be causing that pain?
  •   Do you feel/believe there is anything that can aggravate or alleviate this condition/the pain?
  •   How can you describe it?/How does it feel?/What does it feel like?
  •   How often do you feel that pain?
  •   Where exactly does it hurt?
  •   Is that pain constant or comes and goes/or happens on and off?
  •   Does it radiate to any other place?
  •   On a scale of zero to ten, where zero is no pain at all and ten is the worst possible pain, how would
      you rate your pain?/where would you say the pain is?/can you tell me how severe your pain is?
  • If zero is no pain and ten is the worst pain, where would you place your pain?/How severe is your
    pain on a scale of zero to ten?
  • Are you/Has your child been experiencing any other symptoms? Any headaches? Have you noticed
    anything abnormal on him/her?
  • Sorry, I missed what you said about your pain. Can you please repeat that?
  • But then you started to develop other symptoms?



                                                                                                              2

OET Speaking by Dr Amr Akmal



Asking about history:
  • Have you ever felt anything like that before?
  • Have you ever experienced anything like that before?
  • Have you been taking any medications for this condition? Did it get any better?/So, as far as I
    understand, you are not taking/not compliant to your medications anymore. Is that right?
  • What did your doctor tell you about the diagnosis then?
  • What treatment did you have then?
  • Does any of your family members suffer from any similar condition or any other medical
    problems?/Do you have any family history of any medical condition?
  • Can I ask you some more/a few questions regarding your past medical history if you don’t mind?

Asking for patient’s permission to perform examination:
  •   Would it be okay if I examine you now?
  •   Would you mind if I examine you now?
  •   May I examine you now?
  •   I’d like to examine you, if that’s okay.
  •   If you’re comfortable, I’ll examine you.
  •   To help me understand what’s going on, would it be okay if I examine you?
  •   This will only take a few minutes, and I’ll explain each step as we go.

Requesting investigations:
  •   To get to the bottom of the problem, we need to run some tests.
  •   To get to the bottom of what’s going on, I’d recommend doing some tests.
  •   Given your symptoms, imaging may help us rule out inner ear or nerve-related causes.
  •   This is a precautionary step to make sure we don’t miss anything.
  • At this stage, it’s too early to be certain about a final diagnosis. We’ll need to run some tests,
    including blood tests and liver function tests, to rule out other conditions that can present in a
    similar way.
  • At the moment, it’s too early to confirm a final diagnosis. We need to do some tests, such as blood
    tests and liver function tests, to exclude other conditions that may cause similar symptoms.
  •   An X-ray would help us check the bones and surrounding structures.
  •   I’d recommend an X-ray to rule out any structural problems.
  •   An X-ray is a simple test that can help us identify any abnormalities.
  •   I’d suggest an ultrasound to assess the area more closely.
  •   A CT scan can give us detailed images to help rule out more serious causes.
  •   To get a clearer picture of what’s going on, I’d recommend an MRI. This is mainly to rule out other
      causes and for reassurance. How does that sound to you?

Reaching a diagnosis:
  • Well, thank you for all that background. That's really given me a good idea of what we need to do.
  • Thank you for sharing this information with me. It really helps me understand your situation.


                                                                                                            3

OET Speaking by Dr Amr Akmal



  • From what you’ve told me and from the examination, this looks like aphthous ulcers.
  • Based on your history and initial examination, it appears that you have something/what’s called X
  • What do you already know about your condition?/Have you ever heard of it before?/Have the
    doctors told you anything about your condition and the treatment options? Are you familiar with
    this condition?
  • Would it be okay if I briefly explain what this condition means?
  • Let me explain this in simple terms.
  • We’ll come back to that in a moment, but first, would it be okay if I briefly explain what this condition
    means?
  •   I’ll address that shortly, but first, may I explain what this condition means?
  •   Before we go into that, would it be alright if I explain the condition in simple terms?
  •   I’ll explain that in a moment. First, let me briefly explain what this condition means.
  •   In simple words, bronchial asthma is a lung condition, where.
  •   In simple terms, bronchial asthma is a long-term lung condition where the airways become inflamed
      and narrow, making it difficult to breathe.
  • I’ll try to explain this in simple terms
  • Do you want me to go over that again?
  • Let me see if I can summarize what you’ve said


Giving advice and discussing treatment:
Discussing treatment and assuring patients:
  • Now that we’ve discussed the symptoms and signs of your condition, I would next like to talk to you
    now about the management plan.
  • Now that we’ve talked about your symptoms and examination findings, I’d like to discuss the
    management plan with you. Let’s move on to how we can manage this condition.
  • There are several treatment options available, and I’ll explain each one to you.
  • We have a few ways to manage this, and we’ll choose what suits you best.
  • The good news is that this condition is usually self-limiting.
  • The good news is that this condition is completely manageable with the right treatment.
  • It is contagious, but we can take steps to prevent it from spreading.
  • Most people start to feel better within about two weeks and can gradually return to their normal
    activities.
  •   You should be able to get back to work in around two weeks, depending on your recovery.
  •   Once you start the treatment, you should notice a gradual improvement.
  •   As long as you take the medications as prescribed and get enough rest, you should recover well.
  •   Rest will play a big role in your recovery.

Sympathizing with the patient:
  • I’m really sorry you’re going through this.


                                                                                                                4

OET Speaking by Dr Amr Akmal



  •   That sounds really upsetting for you.
  •   I can see how worried you are.
  •   Anyone in your situation would feel the same.
  •   It’s completely normal to feel this way.
  •   It’s completely understandable to feel this way.
  •   I understand why this is concerning for you.
  •   I’m sorry to hear that.
  •   I understand your concerns/worries.
  •   I understand this must be a hard time for you.
  •   That must have been very difficult/so hard/tough/distressing for you.
  •   I can imagine how stressful this has been.
  •   It sounds like this has been a tough time for your family.
  •   You’ve been dealing with a lot.
  •   As a parent, it’s completely understandable to feel anxious.

Drawing the patient’s attention in a positive way:
  • I know this is hard to hear about your son/daughter, but with the medication and proper rest at
    home, she/he should start to improve.
  • I see that this can be a bit scary, but this is the best treatment option for your case.
  • Right now, the most important thing is helping you recover.
  • Let’s concentrate on what we can do to help you feel better.
  •   I want to reassure you that this condition is quite common.
  •   The good news is that this condition is very manageable.
  •   We see this quite often, and most patients do very well.
  •   Based on my experience, patients usually recover well.
  •   This condition is quite common, and most patients recover fully with proper treatment.
  •   You seem a little uncomfortable about commencing on the medical treatment. Is that right?
  •   You seem a little hesitant about starting the medication. Is that right? Can you tell me what is
      worrying you the most?
  • Is there anything in particular that’s worrying you about the medication?
  • We’ll be monitoring you closely throughout the treatment.
  • We’ll monitor you closely while you’re on this medication, and we will deal promptly with any side
    effects if thy happen.
  • We’ll take this step by step together.

Checking clarity and understanding:
  •   Does that make sense?
  •   Is that clear so far?
  •   Am I explaining this clearly?
  •   Do you understand what I mean?
  •   Does this sound clear to you?



                                                                                                         5

OET Speaking by Dr Amr Akmal



  •   Can I just check that I’ve explained everything clearly?
  •   Could you tell me, in your own words, what you’ve understood so far?
  •   Would you like me to go over that again?
  •   Shall I explain that in a different way?
  •   Are you comfortable with the treatment plan we’ve discussed?
  •   Do you feel clear about how to take the medication?
  •   Is everything clear about when and how to use the treatment?
  •   Do you have any questions about the treatment?
  •   Please feel free to stop me if anything isn’t clear.
  •   If anything doesn’t make sense, just let me know.
  •   What questions do you have at this stage?
  •   How do you feel about what we’ve discussed?
  •   Is there anything you’re still unsure or worried about?
  •   Does this address your main concerns?
  •   Does this answer your question?

Dealing with serious conditions:
  •   I’ve received your pathology report.
  •   I’m afraid the results are more serious than we were hoping for.
  •   The pathology results show that the lesion is malignant, which means it is cancer.
  •   The tests confirm a diagnosis of colon cancer.
  •   Unfortunately, your condition appears to a little bit more serious than we think.
  •   The results show no evidence of colon cancer.
  •   I can imagine this news is very upsetting.
  •   I can imagine how upsetting this must be for you.
  •   I can understand how frustrating this situation is.
  •   I can see how distressed you are.
  •   That must be very difficult for you.
  •   I understand this is a lot to take in. Please take your time and tell me what’s going through your mind
      right now?
  •   Please take your time. What’s going through your mind right now?
  •   There is a lot we can do to manage this.
  •   You are not alone, and we will support you through this.
  •   Effective treatments are available.
  •   Given the nature of the condition, I’d recommend referring you to an oncologist as soon as possible.
  •   Early specialist involvement is important.
  • The good news is that it was detected at an early stage. This significantly improves the chances of
    successful treatment. Treatment is expected to be effective.
  • I understand the idea of surgery can be frightening.
  • Based on current evidence, surgery offers the best chance of cure.
  • Your surgeon will discuss the risks and benefits in detail.



                                                                                                                6

OET Speaking by Dr Amr Akmal



  •   What are your main concerns right now?
  •   Do you have any questions about the diagnosis or next steps?
  •   Would you like me to explain anything again?
  •   I’m afraid the results are more serious than we were hoping for. The biopsy confirms colon cancer. I
      understand this is difficult news, and it’s completely normal to feel overwhelmed. The good news is
      that it was detected early, and there are effective treatment options available. I’d recommend
      referring you to an oncologist to discuss the next steps. What concerns you most at the moment?

Dealing with anxious/stubborn patients:
  • I understand that you might not want to stop taking your sleeping pills, but believe me, I’m
    concerned about your health and general wellbeing.
  • I understand why you feel reluctant to stop your sleeping tablets. My concern is about your long-
    term health, as these medications can be addictive and can also cause many undesirable side effects.
  • Would it be okay if I explain why I’m recommending a change?
  • I understand that you might not feel comfortable about taking this medication. Is that right? Can
    you give me a reason for that? What is making you so concerned or worried? What is
    worrying/concerning you the most?
  • Based on clinical guidelines and experience with similar patients, this treatment is considered one
    of the most effective options. Ultimately, the decision is yours, but I’d strongly recommend this
    approach.
  •   Taking your medication regularly gives us the best chance of controlling your symptoms.
  •   As we know, when it comes to treatment, early intervention is key.
  •   Early treatment usually leads to better outcomes.
  •   I completely understand your worries and concerns, but if we work together and follow the plan,
      we have a very good chance of controlling this condition. My aim is to support you and help you feel
      better.
  • This forms an important part of the treatment plan and is expected to help.
  • If this were a member of my own family, I would feel comfortable recommending this treatment.
  • I understand this is very frustrating, especially when your child is in pain. I can see you’re trying to
    help, and I respect that. My priority is his safety, and that’s why I don’t recommend this option.
  • Well, the benefits generally outweigh any risks, as long as you don't exceed the recommended dose.
    We’ll monitor you closely and adjust the dose if needed.
  • I wouldn't advise/recommend that actually and I’m happy to explain why.

Dealing with patient asking for unnecessary action:
 Sick leave/Medical certificate
  • I understand you’re hoping for some time off.
  • My hands are tied by medical guidelines.
  • I have to work within medical regulations.
  • I can only issue a certificate when it’s clinically indicated.


                                                                                                               7

OET Speaking by Dr Amr Akmal



 •   At the moment, there’s no medical basis for sick leave.
 •   From a medical point of view, you’re fit to work.
 •   I wouldn’t be doing you any favours by issuing a certificate unnecessarily.
 •   I wouldn’t feel comfortable certifying this medically.
 • What I can do is help you manage your symptoms.
 • We can look at other ways to support you.
 • I can understand why you’re asking for a medical certificate. Unfortunately, at this stage there isn’t
   a medical indication for sick leave. My hands are tied by clinical guidelines, but I’m happy to discuss
   ways to help you manage your symptoms.
 • I appreciate this is frustrating, but I wouldn’t feel comfortable issuing a certificate without a clear
   medical reason. I want to be honest and fair with you.
 • At the moment, you’re medically fit to work. However, if your condition worsens, please come back
   and we can reassess.
 • At the moment, there’s no medical indication for sick leave. However, I can help you manage your
   symptoms and feel better. There are several proven strategies to cope with stress, and many patients
   with a similar condition have found significant improvement using them. Would you like me to talk
   you through some of these strategies?
 • I understand why you’re asking for sick leave, but medically there’s no indication for it right now.
   What I can do is help you manage your symptoms. There are effective, evidence-based ways to cope
   with stress, and many patients in a similar situation have improved with these approaches. Would
   you like me to talk you through some of these strategies?

Hospital admission
 • It’s completely understandable to want to be on the safe side.
 • At this stage, hospital admission wouldn’t add any benefit.
 • Right now, admission isn’t medically justified.
 • From a clinical point of view, it’s safe to manage this at home.
 • Keeping you in hospital wouldn’t change the management.
 • My decision is guided by clinical guidelines.
 • Admitting you unnecessarily could actually do more harm than good.
 • What we can do instead is…
 • We’ll arrange close follow-up to check on your progress and how you’re responding to treatment.
 • If anything changes, you should come back immediately.
 • I can understand why you’d feel safer staying in hospital. The good news is that you’re stable and
   there are no red flags, so admission wouldn’t add any benefit. We can safely manage this at home,
   and I’ll explain exactly what to watch out for.”
 • I can see you want to be on the safe side for your child. At the moment, he doesn’t meet the criteria
   for hospital admission, and keeping him here unnecessarily could expose him to other risks. I’ll make
   sure you know when to come back if things change.”




                                                                                                             8

OET Speaking by Dr Amr Akmal



  • I appreciate your concern, but I have to go by medical guidelines. Right now, admission isn’t
    medically justified. What I can do is arrange follow-up and give you clear instructions on when to
    seek urgent help.

Referring the patient:
  • Also, I would recommend referring you to/arranging an appointment with a dietician for a specialist
    opinion. They have specific expertise in managing this condition. A dietitian can help tailor a plan
    that suits your lifestyle and medical needs.
  • How would you feel about seeing a dietitian? Seeking specialist input can be very helpful in
    managing this condition.
  • You’ll receive appropriate care from someone with expertise in this condition.
  • Getting expert advice at this stage can make a big difference.

Taking about lifestyle improvement:
 General questions:
  • How do you feel about making some lifestyle changes, such as exercising more or reducing alcohol?
  • Have you ever thought about adopting a healthier lifestyle?
  • Have you considered starting a regular exercise program or following a healthier diet?

Common Role play scenarios:
Scenario 1: Patient/Relative Requesting Medication Without
Examination
     • Doctor: Good morning. Please have a seat. My name is Dr Amr, and I’ll be looking after
       you today. How can I help?
     • Patient/Relative: I’m here to get a prescription for my father. He’s not feeling well.
     • Doctor: I understand. Can you tell me a bit more about his symptoms and how long he’s
       been unwell?
     • Patient/Relative: He’s had a cough and fever for three days.
     • Doctor: I appreciate you coming in to help. However, I can only prescribe medication after
       examining him myself. This ensures we give the safest and most effective treatment.
     • Patient/Relative: So, you can’t give the medication?
     • Doctor: That’s right. Prescribing without seeing him could be risky, as I wouldn’t know his
       full medical status or potential reactions.
     • Patient/Relative: What can we do then?
     • Doctor: He can come in for an appointment today. If urgent, we’ll see him immediately.
       We could also arrange a telehealth consult, but a physical exam may still be needed
       depending on his symptoms.
     • Patient/Relative: Okay, that sounds good.
     • Doctor: Great. This is for his safety. Do you have any questions about this?

Scenario 2: Explaining a Diagnosis and Treatment Plan (e.g.,
Type 2 Diabetes)
     • Doctor: Hello Mr Smith. Please have a seat. I’d like to discuss the results of your recent
       tests.
     • Patient: Okay, doctor.

General Tips for All OET Speaking Role-Plays:
   • Establish Rapport: Start with a friendly greeting, introduce yourself, and confirm the
     patient's name.
   • Active Listening: Show you're listening by nodding, making eye contact, and using verbal
     affirmations ("I see," "Mm-hmm").
   • Empathy: Acknowledge the patient's feelings and concerns. Use phrases like "I
     understand this must be difficult for you," or "I can see why you're concerned."
   • Clear and Concise Language: Avoid medical jargon. Explain things in simple terms.
   • Structure Your Conversation:
      • Introduction: Greet, introduce, establish purpose.
      • Information Gathering: Ask open-ended questions.


                                                                                                13

OET Speaking by Dr Amr Akmal



        • Explanation/Education: Provide necessary information.
        • Reassurance/Support: Address concerns.
        • Action Plan: Discuss next steps.
        • Checking Understanding: "Does that make sense?" "Do you have any questions?"
        • Closing: Summarize, offer further assistance, say goodbye.

   • Time Management: Keep an eye on the clock (you'll have 5 minutes for the role-play).
     Practice staying within the time limit.
   • Professionalism: Maintain a professional and respectful tone throughout.
   • Confidence: Speak clearly and with conviction.


A Mental Checklist:
  1. Start Properly:
        ❖ The rule:
            •   Greet the patient
            •   Introduce yourself and your role
            •   Confirm the patient’s name
            •   State the purpose

        ❖ Example idioms:
            •   Good morning, I’m Dr Amr, one of the doctors working here today.
            •   Please have a seat.
            •   Could I just confirm your name, please?/How would you like me to address you?
            •   I understand you’re here today because …


  2. Open the Conversation:
        ❖ The rule: Use an open-ended opening question
        ❖ Example idioms:
            • How can I help you today?
            • What brings you in today?
            • I have got some notes here, but perhaps you can tell me in your own words what seems
                to be the problem.


  3. Explore Symptoms / Main Concern:
        ❖ The rule:
            • Ask about onset, duration, severity, associated symptoms
            • Use open questions first

        ❖ Example idioms:
            •   Before we go further, I’d like to ask you a few questions.
            •   To understand this better, can I ask you some questions?
            •   Could you tell me more about that?
            •   When did this start?

            • How does it feel?


  4. Active Listening (Throughout):
        ❖ The rule: Use short verbal acknowledgements
        ❖ Example idioms:
            • I see.
            • Mm-hmm.
            • Right.


  5. Show Empathy After Every Complaint:
        ❖ Rule: No complaint without empathy
        ❖ Example idioms:
            • I’m sorry you’re going through this.
            • I can understand why this is concerning for you.
            • That must be quite uncomfortable


  6. Exclude Red Flags / Underlying Conditions:
        ❖ The rule: Ask focused questions to rule out serious causes
        ❖ Example idioms:
            • Have you ever been diagnosed with…?
            • Have you ever experienced any other symptoms such as…?


  7. Reach the Diagnosis (or Suspected Diagnosis):
        ❖ The rule:
            • State the diagnosis clearly and calmly
            • Use simple language

        ❖ Example idioms:
            • Based on what you’ve told me and my examination…
            • This seems to be most consistent with…


  8. Ask What the Patient Already Knows:
        ❖ The rule: Check prior knowledge before explaining the diagnosis
        ❖ Example idioms:
            • Have you heard of this condition before?
            • What do you already know about it?
            • Can you tell me in your own words what you already know about this condition?


  9. Explain the Condition:
        ❖ The rule: Give short, clear explanations. Avoid medical jargon
        ❖ Example idioms:
            • In simple terms, this means…
            • Basically, what happens is…

 10. Check Understanding After Explanation:
        ❖ Rule: Always check understanding after providing information or an explanation.
        ❖ Example idioms:
            • Does that make sense?
            • Is that clear so far?


 11. Discuss Investigations:
        ❖ The rule: Explain what the test is and why it’s needed
        ❖ Example idioms:
            • I’d recommend a simple test to rule out…
            • This will help us confirm…
            • To further investigate your symptoms, I’d recommend doing some blood tests.


 12. Check Understanding / Agreement for Tests:
        ❖ The rule: Obtain patient agreement
        ❖ Example idioms:
            • Is that okay with you?
            • Are you comfortable to proceed with this?


 13. Management / Treatment Plan:
        ❖ The rule: Explain what to do, how often, and for how long
        ❖ Example idioms:
            • What I’d suggest is…
            • The plan is to start with…


 14. Check Patient’s Opinion After Treatment:
        ❖ Rule: Always check for patient’s opinion after suggesting a treatment plan.
        ❖ Example idioms:
            • How do you feel about this plan?
            • Does that sound reasonable to you?


 15. Reassure and Give Prognosis:
        ❖ The rule: Normalize and reassure when appropriate
        ❖ Example idioms:
            • The good news is…
            • This usually improves on its own.


 16. Lifestyle Advice (If Relevant):
        ❖ The rule: Give practical, simple advice
